title: What Is Cellular Senescence and Can It Be Reversed Naturally - Plasma Therapy
abstract:
## **What Triggers Cellular Senescence in the Human Body**  
Several factors can push cells into senescence, ranging from natural ageing processes to external stressors. Understanding these triggers helps explain why senescence occurs and why some people may experience age-related changes earlier or more severely than others.
## **Current Research on Reversing or Slowing Cellular Senescence**  
The scientific community has made significant strides in understanding whether cellular senescence can be reversed or modified. Animal studies, particularly in mice, have demonstrated successful clearance of senescent cells using various approaches, though the evidence shows this doesn’t always lead to complete functional restoration. [Multiple studies in mice](https://elifesciences.org/articles/75492) show that senolytic drugs can clear senescent cells and improve healthspan, but the evidence suggests that interventions may lead to ‘senescence escape’ without restoring full cellular function.  
However, translating these findings to humans presents substantial challenges. The complexity of human biology, longer lifespans, and ethical considerations around experimental treatments mean that what works in laboratory settings may not directly apply to clinical practice.  
True reversal of cellular senescence remains elusive in humans, but emerging research suggests we may be able to influence the process through targeted interventions that support cellular health and reduce inflammatory burden.  
— Regenerative medicine specialist
### **Experimental Approaches and Laboratory Findings**  
Research has identified several potential pathways for influencing senescence. Some studies have explored compounds that can selectively eliminate senescent cells (called senolytics), while others focus on reducing the inflammatory secretions from these cells (senomorphics). [Laboratory studies](https://lifespan.io/topic/senolytics/) confirm that senolytics can selectively induce cell death in senescent cells while sparing healthy ones, though most evidence remains preclinical.  
One promising area involves targeting metabolic pathways such as mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin), which plays a role in cellular growth and senescence. Laboratory studies using specific mTOR inhibitors have shown some ability to reverse senescence-associated changes in human skin cells, with [controlled studies demonstrating](https://www.aging-us.com/article/100872/text) that pan-mTORC inhibitors can reverse morphological and biochemical features of senescence in human skin fibroblasts within seven days. However, these findings require careful interpretation and further validation.  
Other research has examined how specific lipid compounds might influence senescence in particular cell types, such as pancreatic beta cells involved in diabetes. While these studies offer insights into potential mechanisms, they highlight the tissue-specific nature of senescence and the need for targeted approaches rather than universal solutions.
